title: Why Airtel made its shareholders wait thirteen years
summary: The mirror image of the Mahindra story. Airtel's business grew for over a decade while its stock went almost nowhere. The reason is the single most important idea in investing: a growing business is not the same as a rewarding stock.
intro: In 2007, Bharti Airtel was one of the most admired companies in India, the telecom champion that had brought the mobile phone to the masses. Over the next thirteen years its revenue and its subscriber base grew enormously, it became a household name across two continents, and it never stopped getting bigger. And yet if you had bought the stock in 2007 and held it all the way to 2020, you would have made almost nothing. Thirteen years of waiting, on a business that was growing the entire time.

This is the exact mirror of the Mahindra story. Mahindra's stock fell because the business briefly broke. Airtel's stock went nowhere even though the business kept getting stronger and bigger. Hidden in that contrast is the single most important idea in investing: a growing business and a rewarding stock are not the same thing. The growth was real. The problem was that every rupee of it kept getting eaten, by an acquisition, by capital, by a price war, and by regulation, long before it could ever reach the shareholder.

sections.heading: The paradox, in one line
body: Over these thirteen years Airtel's revenue grew several times over and its customer base exploded into the hundreds of millions. On every measure of size, it was a runaway success. Yet the stock sat still. How can a business grow that much and reward its owners so little?

The answer is that telecom is a machine that devours capital, and Airtel spent the whole decade feeding it. Growth in customers is not the same as growth in profit, and profit that has to be poured straight back into the business, or handed to a lender, or a rival, or the government, is not a return to you. The chapters below are simply the four mouths that ate Airtel's growth, one after another.

sections.heading: Mouth one: the African adventure
body: In March 2010, Airtel made the boldest bet of its life. It bought the African operations of a company called Zain for $10.7 billion, funded almost entirely by debt. The dream was irresistible: take the magic that had conquered India, cheap mobile service for hundreds of millions of new users, and repeat it across more than a dozen African countries. Overnight, net debt swelled toward ₹60,000 crore and the company's gearing jumped from almost nothing to over one times.

Africa turned out to be a very different beast. Many currencies, weaker infrastructure, entrenched rivals like MTN and Vodacom, and a long, grinding fight for profitability. The business bled for years. When Airtel finally listed the African unit on the London Stock Exchange in 2019, the whole thing was valued near $3.9 billion, roughly a third of the $10.7 billion it had paid. A decade of capital and management attention, poured largely into a hole. That debt and those losses hung over the shareholder the entire time.

sections.heading: Mouth two: the treadmill that never stops
body: Even at home, telecom never stops spending. A phone network is only as good as its latest technology and its spectrum, the airwaves that carry the signal, and both cost fortunes. Just as it was digesting the Zain debt, Airtel was bidding billions for 3G spectrum in the 2010 auctions, then 4G after that, then constant upgrades to carry an exploding amount of data.

Spectrum is bought from the government at brutal auctions, and the network needs endless capital just to keep up with demand. So the money actually left over for shareholders after all this spending, the free cash flow, was chronically thin. This is a crucial and unglamorous point: a company can report a profit and still hand its owners almost nothing, if all the cash is being swallowed by the investment needed just to stay in the race.

sections.heading: Mouth three: the Jio earthquake
body: On 5 September 2016, the ground shifted. Reliance Jio, backed by the deepest pockets in India, launched with free voice calls forever and months of free 4G data, then near-zero pricing after that. It was the most aggressive market entry in Indian corporate history, and it was designed to break the incumbents.

To keep its customers from walking to Jio, Airtel had to slash its own prices to match. The lifeblood of any telecom company is its average revenue per user, how much each customer pays a month, and Airtel's collapsed from about ₹202 in 2014 to roughly ₹104. Profits evaporated across the whole industry. Weaker operators died or merged, and a field of about a dozen players was crushed down to just three. Airtel survived, which was itself an achievement, but survival meant years of shrinking profitability while it fought a rival that seemed happy to lose money forever to win.

sections.heading: Mouth four: the regulatory bomb
body: Then came the bill nobody had fully braced for. For years the government and the telecom companies had fought over the definition of "adjusted gross revenue", or AGR, the base of revenue on which the telcos owe the government fees. The companies said it meant only their core telecom revenue; the government said it meant almost everything they earned. On 24 October 2019, the Supreme Court sided completely with the government, and the back-dated dues that suddenly became payable were staggering.

Airtel had to set aside ₹28,450 crore in a single quarter to cover its share. The result was a loss of ₹23,045 crore for the July-to-September 2019 quarter, the largest quarterly loss in the company's history and one of the biggest in Indian corporate history. To see how much of it was the ruling, consider this: without the AGR charge, the loss would have been just ₹1,123 crore. Thirteen years of building a bigger and bigger business, and Airtel was now staring at a government bill large enough to threaten its survival.

sections.heading: And then, at the darkest point, the turn
body: The reward finally came, and it is important to see exactly where it came from, because it was not from growth. Airtel had always had growth. Three things changed at once around 2019 and 2020. The African business, after years of pain, finally reached profitability and its 2019 London listing brought in cash to cut debt. The AGR shock, though brutal, was gradually managed and paid down. And most importantly, the telecom war finally cooled.

With only three players left standing, they could at last behave rationally instead of bleeding each other. In December 2019 came the first real tariff hikes in years, roughly 30 percent, and more followed. Revenue per user began climbing again, and the enormous amount of data that India had become addicted to could finally be charged for properly. Only then, after thirteen years of going nowhere, did the stock break out and begin the powerful multi-year run that rewarded the few who had waited. The reward came not from the business getting bigger, which it always had been, but from it finally being allowed to make money.

timeline.what: Airtel is a market darling at all-time highs, India's telecom champion.
Buys Zain's African operations for $10.7 billion, funded almost entirely by debt.
Bids billions for 3G spectrum; net debt swells toward ₹60,000 crore.
The African unit bleeds; domestic revenue per user grinds lower; the stock goes nowhere.
Reliance Jio launches free voice and data. The price war begins.
Revenue per user collapses from ~₹202 to ~₹104; a dozen operators shrink to three.
Airtel Africa lists in London near $3.9 billion, a third of the $10.7 billion paid.
The Supreme Court's AGR ruling lands.
Airtel posts a ₹23,045 crore quarterly loss, its largest ever.
The first real tariff hikes in years (~30%). The turn begins.
Revenue per user recovers, cash flow returns, and the stock finally re-rates.

lesson: Airtel spent thirteen years proving that a growing business is not the same as a rewarding stock. Its customers and revenue grew the entire time, but that growth was consumed, again and again, by a costly acquisition, an endless capital treadmill, a price war, and a regulatory bill. What finally rewarded shareholders was not more growth, which had always been there. It was the return of pricing power and free cash flow, once the industry consolidated to three players who could at last raise prices. The lesson travels far beyond telecom: never confuse a growing top line with a growing return. Follow the free cash flow per share and the pricing power, because those, not subscriber counts, are what actually reach the shareholder. A wonderful, growing business bought without pricing power can make you wait a very long time.
